A process has its own isolated virtual address space, page tables, file descriptors, and PID, whereas threads within the same process share the virtual memory address space, heap, and open files, each having only their own stack and register set. Context switching overhead differs dramatically because a process context switch requires changing page tables and flushes the TLB, causing significant CPU cache misses. In contrast, a thread context switch preserves the TLB because the address space is shared, making it much cheaper and lightweight.

Threads have their own separate heap memory. A process context switch is only slightly slower than a thread context switch.

Pessimistic locking acquires exclusive locks on rows upfront using SELECT FOR UPDATE, blocking concurrent writers to prevent conflicts; it is best for high-contention write workloads like financial transactions, though it risks deadlocks. Optimistic locking avoids locks upfront, using a version column to check for conflicts at commit time; it is optimal for high-read low-contention systems, but requires retry logic when conflicts occur.
Pessimistic locking locks rows upfront with exclusive locks. Optimistic locking uses a version column to detect conflicts.
Optimistic locking is always faster than pessimistic locking under all circumstances, and pessimistic locking prevents all database deadlocks.

We use Floyd's tortoise and hare with a slow pointer moving 1 step and a fast pointer moving 2 steps; if fast hits null there is no cycle, but if they meet a cycle exists. To find the cycle start, reset one pointer to head and advance both 1 step at a time until they meet at the cycle entry. The mathematical proof shows 2(L + k) - (L + k) = nC so L = nC - k. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space without a visited set.
We use slow and fast pointers moving 1 and 2 steps. When they meet, a cycle exists. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.
The initial meeting point of fast and slow pointers is always the cycle start node directly. The optimal interview solution is to store visited nodes in a HashSet.

An LRU Cache combines a Doubly-Linked List with a HashMap mapping keys to node pointers. For get(key), we look up the node in O(1) and move it to the head. For put(key, value), we update or insert at head, and if over capacity, evict the tail node in O(1). Dummy head and dummy tail sentinel nodes eliminate null pointer edge cases, yielding O(1) time and O(capacity) space.
A singly-linked list with a HashMap achieves O(1) eviction and updates. Alternatively an array with timestamps works in O(1).

B+ Trees store actual data records or row pointers only in leaf nodes, while internal nodes store only routing keys. B+ Tree leaf nodes are linked in a doubly-linked list enabling fast sequential range scans in O(k). Internal nodes without data pointers have much higher fan-out, resulting in a shallower tree and fewer disk I/Os compared to B-Trees which store data at every level.
B-Trees and B+ Trees have identical performance for range queries. Also, B+ Trees store full table rows in internal routing nodes.

The 3-way handshake uses SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK to establish bidirectional connectivity and synchronize initial sequence numbers (ISNs). Three packets are needed because both sides must independently negotiate ISNs and confirm receipt, which two packets cannot guarantee. The 4-way teardown uses FIN and ACK in both directions for half-close, and TIME_WAIT lasts 2MSL to ensure the final ACK was delivered and allow delayed packets to expire.
A 2-way handshake is sufficient to reliably establish a full-duplex TCP connection. Also TIME_WAIT is an error state that indicates a connection leak.

Java 8+ ConcurrentHashMap uses lock-free Compare-And-Swap (CAS) for inserting into empty buckets, and fine-grained synchronized blocks on only the head node of a bucket during collisions. Reads are completely lock-free due to volatile visibility of table nodes. In contrast, Hashtable and synchronizedMap lock the entire table on every read and write.
ConcurrentHashMap uses 16 segment locks in Java 8 and newer, and it acquires a lock during get() operations.

The Java Heap stores live object instances and arrays in managed memory, while Metaspace stores class metadata and bytecode in native off-heap RAM. Metaspace OOM is caused by classloader memory leaks or unbounded dynamic proxy generation like CGLIB, and is diagnosed using jcmd classloader_stats and tuned with MaxMetaspaceSize.
Metaspace is allocated inside the JVM heap space, and Metaspace stores static variables in Java 8+.

N+1 select occurs when 1 query for parent records triggers N additional secondary queries for child associations. We solve it using JPQL JOIN FETCH to join entities in one SQL query or via Spring Data @EntityGraph on repository methods. FetchType.EAGER does not solve it because JPQL parses the root entity first and fires subsequent queries anyway.
Setting FetchType.EAGER in entity annotations resolves the N+1 select problem, and JOIN FETCH can be applied to multiple @OneToMany lists without any risk.
